Plausibility bounds for the SD of bounded questionnaire scores

An analytic method, its validation, and the functions in the strait package

Author
Affiliation

Ian Hussey

University of Bern

The question

A paper reports a mean of 25 and an SD of 8 on the BDI-II (0–63) for \(N = 50\) people. Is that SD plausible?

Hard bounds answer a narrower question: is the SD possible? The largest possible SD comes from putting as many scores as possible at the two scale limits (Muilwijk, 1966; Bhatia & Davis, 2000). The smallest comes from putting all scores on the two integers next to the mean. For this example the hard range is about 0 to 31. Nearly every SD a real paper reports passes.

Plausibility bounds ask what a realistic data-generating process would produce: the range of sample SDs you would see at this mean and \(N\) if the scores came from the kind of distribution that questionnaire data actually follow. An SD far outside that range is not impossible, but it is surprising enough to warrant a closer look.

The previous approach was simulation. Fit beta-binomial regressions to a corpus of raw BDI-II data, predict the dispersion at each mean, sample from that beta-binomial at each \(N\), and take the 1% and 0.1% quantiles of the sample SD. This document replaces the simulation with analytic and exact calculations, and validates them.

The model

Scores are \(X = \text{score} - L \in \{0, \dots, m\}\) with \(m = U - L\) (\(m = 63\) for the BDI-II). They are modelled as

\[ X \sim \text{BetaBinomial}(m, \alpha, \beta), \qquad \mu = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha + \beta}, \qquad \rho = \frac{1}{\alpha + \beta + 1}, \]

so that

\[ E[X] = m\mu, \qquad \sigma^2 = m\mu(1 - \mu)\,[1 + (m - 1)\rho]. \]

\(\rho\) is the intra-class correlation of the \(m\) Bernoulli trials behind the score. \(\rho = 0\) is the binomial, the least dispersed member of the family. As \(\rho \to 1\), all mass moves to the two endpoints. All population moments are computed exactly from the pmf, \(\log p(x) = \log\binom{m}{x} + \log B(x + \alpha, m - x + \beta) - \log B(\alpha, \beta)\), rather than from closed forms:

bb_cumulants(m = 63, mu = 25 / 63, rho = 0.052)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 8
#>    mean    k2    k3    k4     k5     k6    g1     g2
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1    25  63.7  93.7 -977. -9136. 67824. 0.184 -0.241

Estimating the dispersion from summary statistics

Given a reported \((L, U, M, SD)\), the method of moments gives

\[ \hat\mu = \frac{M - L}{m}, \qquad \hat\rho = \frac{1}{m - 1}\left[\frac{SD^2}{m\hat\mu(1 - \hat\mu)} - 1\right]. \]

\(\hat\rho\) is linear in \(S^2\), so it is unbiased for \(\rho\) given \(\mu\), and its sampling variance is \(\operatorname{Var}(S^2)/[m(m - 1)\mu(1 - \mu)]^2\). Negative \(\hat\rho\) are kept: truncating them would bias a corpus average upward.

rho_from_summary(L = 0, U = 63, M = 25, SD = 8, N = 50)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#>   mu_hat rho_hat  var_rho
#>    <dbl>   <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1  0.397  0.0523 0.000169

Using a paper’s own SD to set \(\rho\) and then checking that same SD is circular, and the functions allow it only for illustration. In practice \(\rho\) comes from a corpus (see Estimating ρ from a corpus).

The sampling distribution of the sample SD

Two moments

For any iid process with a finite fourth moment, the unbiased sample variance satisfies

\[ E[S^2] = \sigma^2, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(S^2) = \sigma^4\left[\frac{2}{N - 1} + \frac{\gamma_2}{N}\right], \qquad \gamma_2 = \frac{\mu_4}{\sigma^4} - 3 . \]

The two-moment approximation (Box, 1954; Satterthwaite, 1946) matches these with a scaled chi-square:

\[ S^2 \approx \sigma^2\,\frac{\chi^2_\nu}{\nu}, \qquad \nu = \frac{2}{2/(N - 1) + \gamma_2/N}, \qquad q_p(S) = \sigma\sqrt{\chi^2_{\nu,p}/\nu}. \]

With normal data, \(\gamma_2 = 0\) and \(\nu = N - 1\), the textbook result. Because \(\gamma_2 \ge -2\) for any distribution, the denominator is always positive. The approximation reproduces the reference table exactly:

ref <- sd_plausibility(0, 63, M = 25, N = c(20, 50, 100, 500),
                       p = c(0.01, 0.001), sd = 8)
ref[, c("N", "p", "rho", "sigma", "hard_min", "hard_max", "lower", "upper")]
#> # A tibble: 8 x 8
#>       N     p    rho sigma hard_min hard_max lower upper
#>   <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1    20 0.01  0.0523  8.00        0     31.4  5.24 10.9 
#> 2    20 0.001 0.0523  8.00        0     31.4  4.47 11.9 
#> 3    50 0.01  0.0523  8.00        0     31.0  6.26  9.78
#> 4    50 0.001 0.0523  8.00        0     31.0  5.74 10.4 
#> 5   100 0.01  0.0523  8.00        0     30.8  6.77  9.25
#> 6   100 0.001 0.0523  8.00        0     30.8  6.39  9.68
#> 7   500 0.01  0.0523  8.00        0     30.8  7.45  8.55
#> 8   500 0.001 0.0523  8.00        0     30.8  7.27  8.74

Three moments

The two-moment approximation gets the skewness of \(S^2\) right only for normal-like data. The third cumulant of \(S^2\), in terms of the population cumulants \(\kappa_2, \dots, \kappa_6\), is

\[ \kappa_3(S^2) = \frac{\kappa_6}{N^2} + \frac{12\kappa_2\kappa_4}{N(N - 1)} + \frac{4(N - 2)\kappa_3^2}{N(N - 1)^2} + \frac{8\kappa_2^3}{(N - 1)^2}. \]

For normal data this is \(8\sigma^6/(N - 1)^2\), the third cumulant of \(\sigma^2\chi^2_{N-1}/(N-1)\). The test suite checks the formula against the exact distribution below, and it agrees to machine precision. Two refinements use it:

  • Cornish–Fisher (method = "cf"): \(q_p(S^2) \approx \kappa_1 + \sqrt{\kappa_2}\,[z_p + \tfrac{\gamma}{6}(z_p^2 - 1)]\), with \(\gamma = \kappa_3/\kappa_2^{3/2}\) the skewness of \(S^2\). The CDF is obtained by solving the quadratic in \(z\), which is needed for the mixture below.
  • Three-moment chi-square (method = "chisq3"): \(S^2 \approx a + b\chi^2_\nu\) with \(b = \kappa_3/(4\kappa_2)\), \(\nu = 8\kappa_2^3/\kappa_3^2\) and \(a = \kappa_1 - b\nu\) (a Pearson type III fit). It keeps the chi-square shape, so it behaves better than Cornish–Fisher in the far tails.

Exact, by dynamic programming

Because \(X\) is a bounded integer, the exact distribution of \(S^2 = [\sum X^2 - (\sum X)^2/N]/(N - 1)\) follows from the joint distribution of \((T, Q) = (\sum X, \sum X^2)\). That joint distribution builds up one observation at a time:

\[ P_{n+1}(t, q) = \sum_{x=0}^{m} p(x)\, P_n(t - x,\ q - x^2). \]

For each sum \(t\), \(q\) lies between the most even split of \(t\) over \(n\) values and the most extreme one, so the state is stored as one vector per \(t\) over that range (s2_exact()). The cost grows roughly as \(N^2 m^3\). On a 0–63 scale the method is practical up to about \(N = 25\): \(N = 20\) takes under a minute. Values and sums with probability below \(10^{-17}\) are pruned, and the discarded mass is reported (below \(10^{-14}\) throughout the validation). The exact method is the ground truth for small \(N\), and it also gives the distribution conditional on the sample mean, which matters below.

Heterogeneity: mixing over ρ

A corpus meta-regression predicts a mean \(\rho\) at each \(\mu\) and a between-study SD \(\tau\). The plausibility bound is then a quantile of the mixture over \(\rho \sim N(\rho, \tau^2)\) truncated to \([0, 1)\):

\[ F_S(s) = \int F_S(s \mid \rho)\, \mathrm{d}G(\rho), \qquad \text{bound} = F_S^{-1}(p). \]

sd_plausibility() represents \(G\) by \(K\) equal-weight quantile nodes of the truncated normal. It averages the per-node CDFs and inverts the average. Averaging per-node quantiles would be wrong, because the quantile of a mixture is not the mixture of quantiles.

sd_plausibility(0, 63, M = 25, N = 50, p = 0.001, rho = 0.052,
                tau = c(0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.04))[, c("tau", "lower", "upper")]
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>     tau lower upper
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1  0     5.72  10.4
#> 2  0.01  5.24  11.0
#> 3  0.02  4.03  12.1
#> 4  0.04  3.42  14.1

Hard bounds

The plausibility bounds are reported next to the hard bounds, and clipped to them:

  • Ceiling: the sharp mean-conditional maximum for integer data, sd_max_structure_s(): as many scores as possible at the two limits, with at most one in between (Mestdagh et al., 2018). This is never above the Bhatia–Davis bound \(\sqrt{N/(N-1)\,(M - L)(U - M)}\).
  • Floor: the minimum variance over integer vectors of length \(N\) with mean \(M\). It puts every score on the two integers next to \(M\): with \(f\) the fractional part of \(M - L\), \(SD_{\min} = \sqrt{N/(N - 1)}\sqrt{f(1 - f)}\) (sd_min_integer()). With digits, the floor is the minimum over every integer sum whose mean rounds to the reported \(M\). When no integer sample has mean \(M\) exactly, the quasi-integer floor is used, which is valid at every real mean.

Validation

The approximations were compared with ground truth on the grid in the spec: \(m = 63\), \(\mu \in \{0.1, 0.3, 0.5\}\), \(\rho \in \{0.02, 0.05, 0.15\}\), \(N \in \{10, 20, 50, 200\}\), at the 1% and 0.1% quantiles in each tail. That is 144 quantiles per method. The ground truth is the exact distribution where \(N \le 20\), and Monte Carlo with \(10^6\) replicates otherwise. The replicates are sampled as multinomial counts, so the cost does not grow with \(N\). The script is dev/sd-plausibility-bounds/validate.R.

Monte Carlo agrees with the exact method wherever both exist. The median 95% half-width of a Monte Carlo quantile is 0.14%. The largest difference between the two, 2.6%, is one step of discreteness: at \(\mu = 0.1\), \(N = 10\), the attainable SDs next to the 0.1% quantile are 1.197 and 1.229, and the Monte Carlo quantile landed on the second. Where the ground truth is Monte Carlo (\(N \ge 50\)), errors below about 1% cannot be resolved.

summ <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("chisq2", "chisq3", "cf"), function(meth) {
  e <- val[[paste0("rel_", meth)]]
  do.call(rbind, lapply(split(seq_len(nrow(val)), list(val$tail, val$p)),
    function(i) data.frame(
      method = meth, tail = val$tail[i[1]], p = val$p[i[1]],
      over_2pct = sum(abs(e[i]) > 0.02), of = length(i),
      max_abs_error = pct(max(abs(e[i])), 1))))
}))
rownames(summ) <- NULL
knitr::kable(summ)
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("chisq2", "chisq3", "cf"), function(meth) {
  data.frame(val[c("mu", "rho", "N", "tail", "p")], method = meth,
             err = val[[paste0("rel_", meth)]])
}))
long$quantile <- paste0(long$tail, " ", long$p * 100, "%")
ggplot(long, aes(factor(N), err, colour = method)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -0.02, ymax = 0.02,
           alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), size = 1.3, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~quantile, nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(100 * x, "%")) +
  labs(x = "N", y = "relative error", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
worst <- val[abs(val$rel_chisq2) > 0.02,
             c("mu", "rho", "N", "tail", "p", "truth",
               "rel_chisq2", "rel_chisq3", "rel_cf")]
worst <- worst[order(-abs(worst$rel_chisq2)), ]
worst$truth <- round(worst$truth, 2)
for (v in c("rel_chisq2", "rel_chisq3", "rel_cf")) worst[[v]] <- pct(worst[[v]])
rownames(worst) <- NULL
knitr::kable(worst)

Three results stand out.

The two-moment method is reliable at large N and in the upper tail. All 36 of its quantiles at \(N = 200\) are within 2% of the truth. In the upper tail its largest error at any \(N\) is 4.5%. Its failures are concentrated where the plan expected them: small \(N\), extreme tails, and specifically the lower tail of a skewed score distribution. At \(\mu = 0.1\), \(N = 10\), it puts the 0.1% lower bound 29% too low.

The moment refinements fix the upper tail but not the lower one. The three-moment chi-square and Cornish–Fisher bring every upper-tail quantile within 2%. In the lower tail at \(N \le 20\) they are no better than the two-moment method, and in several cells worse. The three-moment fit returns 0 in one cell because its fitted shift is negative, and Cornish–Fisher overshoots by up to 64%. This is not a matter of adding another cumulant. At small \(N\) the lower tail of \(S\) is lumpy (a few attainable values carry all the mass) and bounded below, which no smooth moment-matched curve represents well.

For \(N \le 20\), the exact method is the answer. It takes seconds at \(N = 10\) and about a minute at \(N = 20\) on a 0–63 scale, and it has no approximation error to validate.

Review of the plan

The plan is sound: a two-moment approximation with exact moments from the pmf, a mixture over \(\rho\) done on the CDF scale, and exact small-\(N\) ground truth. Working it through raised six points. Two of them change results.

1. Condition on the reported mean

This is the most consequential point. A reported SD comes with a reported mean. The bounds above describe samples of size \(N\) in general, whose means scatter around \(m\mu\). For a skewed distribution, \(S^2\) and \(\bar X\) are correlated: exactly, \(\operatorname{Cov}(\bar X, S^2) = \kappa_3/N\). Samples whose mean happens to land at \(M\) have a narrower SD distribution than samples in general. The question a forensic check asks is the conditional one: given that this sample’s mean is \(M\), how surprising is its SD?

Removing the part of \(\operatorname{Var}(S^2)\) explained by \(\bar X\) gives, to leading order,

\[ \operatorname{Var}(S^2 \mid \bar X = \mu) \approx \operatorname{Var}(S^2) - \frac{\kappa_3^2}{N\sigma^2} = \sigma^4\left[\frac{2}{N - 1} + \frac{\gamma_2 - \gamma_1^2}{N}\right], \]

which is the unconditional formula with \(\gamma_2\) replaced by \(\gamma_2 - \gamma_1^2\). Pearson’s inequality (\(\gamma_2 \ge \gamma_1^2 - 2\)) keeps it positive. The two-moment method uses this with condition_on_mean = TRUE. The exact method conditions directly, on the sums whose mean rounds to the reported \(M\).

The exact distribution shows how large the effect is. Let the shift be the relative change in a bound when conditioning on the mean. At \(\mu = 0.5\) the score distribution is symmetric, \(\gamma_1 = 0\), and the leading-order correction vanishes. The exact shift is still up to 3%, a second-order effect at \(N \le 20\). At \(\mu = 0.3\) the shift is up to 13%. At \(\mu = 0.1\), the regime of depression scales in community samples, it is up to 150%. For \(\rho = 0.15\) and \(N = 10\) the conditional 0.1% lower bound is 3.13 against 1.25 unconditionally, and the conditional upper bound is 14.1 against 16.8. Measured against the conditional truth, the unconditional two-moment bounds are off by up to 71%.

The conditional two-moment correction recovers most of this: its largest error against the exact conditional distribution is 22%. What remains is the small-\(N\) lower-tail problem from the validation. The conditional correction has only been checked against exact results up to \(N = 20\), where exact is available anyway. Its error shrinks with \(N\) (the correction is exact to leading order as \(N \to \infty\)), but its accuracy at \(N = 50\) is not yet verified.

w <- val[val$N <= 20 & val$p == 0.001, ]
wid <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(w, list(w$mu, w$rho, w$N), drop = TRUE), function(d) {
  lo <- d[d$tail == "lower", ]; hi <- d[d$tail == "upper", ]
  data.frame(mu = lo$mu, rho = lo$rho, N = lo$N,
             unconditional = hi$exact - lo$exact,
             conditional = hi$exact_cond - lo$exact_cond)
}))
wid$ratio <- wid$conditional / wid$unconditional
ggplot(wid, aes(factor(rho), ratio, colour = factor(mu), group = mu)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ paste0("N = ", N)) +
  labs(x = expression(rho), y = "conditional / unconditional width",
       colour = expression(mu))

2. The binomial floor is not a floor for the sample SD

The plan lists as a defect that at small \(N\) the lower quantile can fall below \(\sigma_{\text{binom}} = \sqrt{m\mu(1 - \mu)}\), “impossible under the model”. It is not impossible. \(\sigma_{\text{binom}}\) is a floor on the population SD across the family (\(\rho \ge 0\)). A sample SD fluctuates around its population value, and it falls below \(\sigma_{\text{binom}}\) often. The exact distribution shows this directly. Across the validation grid at \(N = 10\), the exact probability that \(S < \sigma_{\text{binom}}\) ranges from 0.01% to 11.5%. Whenever it exceeds \(p\), the true lower quantile lies below \(\sigma_{\text{binom}}\): this holds for 20 of the 36 exact lower quantiles. Clipping to \(\sigma_{\text{binom}}\) would make those lower bounds wrong.

The real constraint is the hard integer floor (item 6 of the plan), and that is what the functions clip to. They also report when clipping happened (clipped, note). With a 64-point scale the floor is rarely binding, because it never exceeds \(0.5\sqrt{N/(N-1)}\). It binds on short scales at tiny \(N\):

sd_plausibility(0, 2, M = 0.5, N = 4, rho = 0, p = 0.01, method = "chisq2")[
  , c("sigma", "hard_min", "lower", "upper", "clipped")]
#> # A tibble: 1 x 5
#>   sigma hard_min lower upper clipped    
#>   <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr>      
#> 1 0.612    0.577 0.577     1 lower+upper

3. Truncate the ρ distribution, do not clamp it

The starting implementation clamped the \(\rho\) nodes with pmin(pmax(...)). That puts a point mass at 0 (and near 1) rather than truncating. When \(\rho\) is small relative to \(\tau\), which is common, a large share of the nodes collapse onto the binomial. The implementation now places the nodes at the quantiles of the truncated normal, as the plan describes.

old_nodes <- function(rho, tau, K = 41)
  pmin(pmax(qnorm((seq_len(K) - 0.5) / K, rho, tau), 0), 1 - 1e-6)
c(clamped_share_at_zero = mean(old_nodes(0.02, 0.03) == 0),
  truncated_share_at_zero = mean(strait:::.rho_nodes(0.02, 0.03, 41) == 0))
#>   clamped_share_at_zero truncated_share_at_zero 
#>               0.2439024               0.0000000

4. Include the prediction’s own uncertainty

\(\tau\) from a meta-regression is the residual between-study SD around the fitted curve. The fitted \(\rho\) at a given \(\mu\) is itself estimated, and its standard error is not part of \(\tau\). For a new study, the relevant spread is the prediction interval’s: \(\tau_{\text{total}} = \sqrt{\tau^2 + \mathrm{SE}^2}\). predict() on a corpus fit returns both, and tau_total is the one to pass to sd_plausibility(). In the simulated corpus below, SE is small next to \(\tau\) in the middle of the \(\mu\) range. It grows towards the ends, where the spline has less data.

5. The variance of ρ̂ treats μ as known

\(\operatorname{Var}(\hat\rho)\) uses \(\operatorname{Var}(S^2)\) only. \(\hat\mu\) is estimated too, and \(\hat\rho\) depends on it through \(\mu(1 - \mu)\). The extra delta-method term is of order \(1/N\) and is small next to \(\operatorname{Var}(S^2)\), except near the scale limits, where \(\mu(1 - \mu)\) is small and changes quickly. This only affects the weights in the meta-regression. The implementation leaves it out and documents the omission.

6. The kurtosis cannot be checked from summary statistics

This caveat is the plan’s own, and it is the one that matters most for interpretation. The bounds depend on the data-generating process mainly through \(\gamma_2\) (and, conditionally, through \(\gamma_2 - \gamma_1^2\)). The beta-binomial fixes both once \(\mu\) and \(\rho\) are fixed. A corpus of means and SDs identifies \(\rho\) but says nothing about whether real scores have beta-binomial tails. Floor effects, zero inflation and bimodality all change the kurtosis at a given \((\mu, \rho)\), and so change the bounds. Checking this needs raw data: a corpus of raw scores, or at least published histograms. Until then, the bounds are plausibility bounds under the beta-binomial, and should be described that way.

cu <- strait:::.cumulants_from_pmf(strait:::.bb_pmf(63, 25 / 63, 0.052))
g2s <- seq(-1.2, 3, by = 0.1)
kb <- do.call(rbind, lapply(g2s, function(g2) {
  sc <- strait:::.s2_cumulants(modifyList(cu, list(g2 = g2)), 50)
  nu <- 2 * sc$k1^2 / sc$k2
  data.frame(g2 = g2,
             lower = sqrt(sc$k1 * qchisq(0.001, nu) / nu),
             upper = sqrt(sc$k1 * qchisq(0.999, nu) / nu))
}))
ggplot(kb, aes(g2)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.2, fill = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_line(aes(y = lower)) + geom_line(aes(y = upper)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cu$g2, linetype = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = cu$g2, y = max(kb$upper), label = " beta-binomial",
           hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 3.5) +
  labs(x = expression("population excess kurtosis " * gamma[2]),
       y = "plausible SD")

Estimating ρ from a corpus

rho_corpus_fit() needs only summary statistics: one row per study with \((L, U, M, SD, N)\). It computes each study’s \((\hat\mu_i, \hat\rho_i, \operatorname{Var}(\hat\rho_i))\) and fits a random-effects meta-regression of \(\hat\rho_i\) on a natural spline in \(\hat\mu_i\) with metafor::rma() (Viechtbauer, 2010). \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat\rho_i)\) depends on the kurtosis at \((\mu_i, \rho_i)\). It is first evaluated at \(\max(0, \hat\rho_i)\), then once more at the fitted curve, and the model is refitted. The second pass matters because a noisy \(\hat\rho_i\) gives a noisy weight.

The corpus below is simulated. It has 150 studies on a 0–63 scale with a true \(\rho(\mu)\) that rises towards the floor, as depression scales do, between-study SD \(\tau = 0.015\), and sample SDs drawn from the model.

set.seed(11)
true_rho <- function(mu) 0.03 + 0.06 * exp(-8 * mu)
k <- 150
mu_i <- runif(k, 0.08, 0.7)
N_i <- sample(30:400, k, replace = TRUE)
rho_i <- pmax(0, true_rho(mu_i) + rnorm(k, 0, 0.015))
SD_i <- vapply(seq_len(k), function(i) {
  pr <- strait:::.bb_pmf(63, mu_i[i], rho_i[i])
  x <- sample(0:63, N_i[i], replace = TRUE, prob = pr)
  sd(x)
}, 0)
corpus <- data.frame(L = 0, U = 63, M = 63 * mu_i, SD = SD_i, N = N_i)
fit <- rho_corpus_fit(corpus)
fit
#> Corpus meta-regression of rho on mu (150 studies, natural spline df = 3)
#>   tau (between-study SD of rho): 0.0149
grid_mu <- seq(0.08, 0.7, length.out = 100)
pr <- predict(fit, grid_mu)
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = fit$data, aes(mu_hat, rho_hat, size = 1 / var_rho),
             alpha = 0.35, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_ribbon(data = pr, aes(mu, ymin = rho - 1.96 * tau_total,
                             ymax = rho + 1.96 * tau_total),
              alpha = 0.2, fill = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_line(data = pr, aes(mu, rho), colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_line(aes(grid_mu, true_rho(grid_mu)), linetype = 2) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 3) +
  labs(x = expression(hat(mu)), y = expression(hat(rho)))

The corpus prediction then feeds sd_plausibility(). Here is the check for the example report (M = 25, SD = 8, N = 50):

p25 <- predict(fit, 25 / 63)
p25
#> # A tibble: 1 x 5
#>      mu    rho      se    tau tau_total
#>   <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 0.397 0.0349 0.00209 0.0149    0.0150
sd_plausibility(0, 63, M = 25, N = 50, p = c(0.01, 0.001),
                rho = p25$rho, tau = p25$tau_total,
                condition_on_mean = TRUE)[
  , c("p", "rho", "tau", "sigma", "lower", "upper")]
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>       p    rho    tau sigma lower upper
#>   <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 0.01  0.0349 0.0150  6.91  4.16  9.61
#> 2 0.001 0.0349 0.0150  6.91  3.62 10.5

Recommendations

  • Condition on the reported mean (condition_on_mean = TRUE). This matters more than the choice of approximation whenever the score distribution is skewed.
  • For \(N \le 20\) on scales of this length, use method = "exact". It is exact, conditions on the reported mean at its reported precision (digits), and costs seconds to a minute.
  • Above that, use method = "chisq2" with condition_on_mean = TRUE. Its upper bound is reliable. Treat its lower bound with caution at moderate \(N\). For skewed distributions (\(\mu\) near 0 or 1) it runs too low, which is conservative for flagging a small SD. For symmetric, strongly dispersed ones (\(\mu = 0.5\), \(\rho = 0.15\)) it runs too high, which is not.
  • A three-moment conditional approximation would need the conditional third cumulant of \(S^2\). That derivation is the natural next step, and it could be validated with a faster exact DP (for example, in C++) at \(N = 50\).
  • Take \(\rho\) and \(\tau\) from a corpus, pass tau_total, and never set \(\rho\) from the SD being checked.
  • Report the bounds as plausible under the beta-binomial, and treat a report outside them as a prompt for a closer look, not as a verdict.

Function reference

Function Purpose
sd_plausibility(L, U, M, N, p, rho, tau, sd, method, condition_on_mean, digits, K) Plausibility bounds, with hard bounds, clipping and notes. Vectorised over M, N, rho, tau, sd (recycled together) and p (crossed).
s2_exact(m, mu, rho, N, sums) Exact distribution of \(S^2\) by dynamic programming, optionally conditional on the sum.
bb_cumulants(m, mu, rho) Mean, cumulants \(\kappa_2\)–\(\kappa_6\), \(\gamma_1\) and \(\gamma_2\) from the pmf.
rho_from_summary(L, U, M, SD, N) Method-of-moments \(\hat\mu\), \(\hat\rho\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat\rho)\).
rho_corpus_fit(corpus, df) / predict(fit, mu) Corpus meta-regression of \(\hat\rho\) on \(\hat\mu\); predicted \(\rho\), SE, \(\tau\) and \(\tau_{\text{total}}\).

Edge cases: a mean at a scale limit returns zero bounds with a note. A mean outside the scale, \(N < 2\), or a missing input returns NA with a note. \(\rho < 0\) (under-dispersed) is computed at the binomial, with a note. \(\rho \ge 1\) uses the endpoint-only limit. U - L must be a whole number, so a mean-scored scale must be converted to sum scores first.
